questions.q: Which tuple is the formal definition of a deterministic finite automaton?
questions.explain: A DFA is a 5-tuple: set of states Q, alphabet Σ, transition function δ, initial state q0, and set of final states F.

questions.q: A DFA must have at least one final state.
questions.explain: The only constraint on F is F ⊆ Q. F = ∅ is allowed. Such a machine accepts nothing, so its language is ∅.

questions.q: The definition of a DFA allows every one of its states to be final (F = Q).
questions.explain: Q is a subset of itself, so F = Q satisfies F ⊆ Q.

questions.q: What is the only constraint the DFA definition places on the set of final states F?
choices: F must contain exactly one state
questions.explain: F just has to be a subset of Q. It may be empty, it may contain q0, and it may contain any number of states.

questions.q: Which of these are requirements of the formal definition of a DFA?
choices: q0 is an element of Q
F is a subset of Q
δ gives exactly one state for every (state, symbol) pair
F contains at least one state
q0 is not a final state
questions.explain: q0 ∈ Q, F ⊆ Q, Q is finite, and δ : Q × Σ → Q is a function. F may be empty, and q0 may be final.

questions.q: A machine over Σ = {a, b} with a single state q1, which is both initial and final and loops to itself on a and on b, is a DFA.
questions.explain: Q = {q1}, q0 = q1, F = {q1}, δ(q1, a) = q1 and δ(q1, b) = q1. Every (state, symbol) pair has exactly one result, so it meets the definition even though it looks odd.

questions.q: A DFA has 7 states and the alphabet {a, b, c}. How many transitions (arrows) must it have?
questions.explain: δ must be defined on every pair in Q × Σ, so the count is |Q| × |Σ| = 7 × 3 = 21.

questions.q: A DFA over the alphabet {a, b} has exactly 14 transitions. How many states does it have?
questions.explain: Transitions = |Q| × |Σ|, so 14 = |Q| × 2 and |Q| = 7.

questions.q: What is the domain of a DFA's transition function δ?
questions.explain: δ : Q × Σ → Q. It takes a (state, symbol) pair and returns a state.

questions.q: A diagram over Σ = {a, b} shows state q2 with one arrow labeled b going to q2 and another arrow labeled b going to q1. Why is this alone enough to make the diagram not a DFA?
choices: δ(q2, b) would have two values, so δ is not a function
Self-loops are not allowed in a DFA's state diagram
A state cannot have an arrow back to an earlier state
The symbol b may label only one arrow in the whole machine
questions.explain: A function assigns one and only one value to each element of its domain. Here δ(q2, b) = q2 and δ(q2, b) = q1, so δ is a relation, not a function.

questions.q: If some state has no outgoing arrow for a symbol, the diagram is still a DFA, as long as no state has two arrows for the same symbol.
questions.explain: δ must be defined for every (state, symbol) pair. A missing transition alone means the machine is not a DFA.

questions.q: If δ assigns two different states to the same (state, symbol) pair, δ is only a relation. What kind of mathematical object does the DFA definition require δ to be?
questions.explain: δ must be a function: it assigns exactly one state to every element of Q × Σ.

questions.q: In the vending machine DFA from class, Σ = {quarter, half-dollar} and each state is named by the amount deposited so far. Starting from the 0 deposited state, what is δ(0, half-dollar)?
questions.explain: Reading a half-dollar from 0 deposited moves the machine to the 50¢ deposited state. (δ(0, quarter) is 25¢ deposited.)

questions.q: M has states q0 (initial) and q1 (final) over Σ = {a, b}, with δ(q0, a) = q1, δ(q0, b) = q0, δ(q1, a) = q0, δ(q1, b) = q1. What happens when M reads baab?
questions.explain: q0 -b→ q0 -a→ q1 -a→ q0 -b→ q0. q0 is not final, so baab is rejected. It has two a's, and this machine accepts strings with an odd number of a's.

questions.q: M over Σ = {a, b} has states q0 (initial), q1, and q2 (final), with δ(q0, a) = q1, δ(q0, b) = q0, δ(q1, a) = q2, δ(q1, b) = q0, δ(q2, a) = q2, δ(q2, b) = q2. M accepts ababa.
questions.explain: q0 -a→ q1 -b→ q0 -a→ q1 -b→ q0 -a→ q1. q1 is not final, so ababa is rejected. It never contains aa.

questions.q: M over Σ = {a, b} has states q0 (initial), q1, q2 (final), and q3, with δ(q0, a) = q1, δ(q0, b) = q3, δ(q1, a) = q1, δ(q1, b) = q2, δ(q2, a) = q3, δ(q2, b) = q2, δ(q3, a) = q3, δ(q3, b) = q3. In which state does M finish after reading abab?
questions.explain: q0 -a→ q1 -b→ q2 -a→ q3 -b→ q3. Once in the trap state q3, the machine never leaves, so abab is rejected.

questions.q: M over Σ = {a, b} has states q0 (initial), q1, q2 (final), and q3, with δ(q0, a) = q1, δ(q0, b) = q3, δ(q1, a) = q1, δ(q1, b) = q2, δ(q2, a) = q3, δ(q2, b) = q2, δ(q3, a) = q3, δ(q3, b) = q3. Which strings does M accept?
questions.explain: M accepts a⁺b⁺: one or more a's followed by one or more b's. ba and abba end in the trap q3, a ends in the non-final q1, and λ leaves M in the non-final q0.

questions.q: A DFA accepts a string as soon as it enters a final state, even if some input symbols have not been read yet.
questions.explain: The computation ends only when the entire string has been consumed. The string is accepted if the state at that point is final.

questions.q: When does a DFA's computation on an input string terminate?
choices: When the entire input string has been consumed
As soon as the machine enters a final state
When the machine enters a trap state
When the machine returns to the initial state
questions.explain: The machine reads every symbol. Only then does it accept (final state) or reject (non-final state).

questions.q: A DFA over Σ = {a, b} has one state, which is initial, loops on both a and b, and is not final (F = ∅). What is its language?
questions.explain: With no final states, nothing is accepted, not even λ. The language is ∅, which is a valid language because it is a subset of Σ*.

questions.q: The empty language ∅ and the language {λ} are the same language.
questions.explain: ∅ contains no strings at all. {λ} contains exactly one string, the empty string.

questions.q: M over Σ = {a, b} has q0 (initial and final) and q1 (not final), with δ(q0, a) = δ(q0, b) = q1 and δ(q1, a) = δ(q1, b) = q0. Which describes L(M)?
choices: Strings of even length, including λ
Strings of even length, excluding λ
Strings with an even number of a's
questions.explain: Every symbol switches the state, so q0 means even length so far. q0 is final, so λ (length 0) is accepted too.

questions.q: A DFA over Σ = {a, b} has exactly one state. Which of these languages could it accept?
questions.explain: With one state, both symbols must loop back to it. If the state is final the language is Σ*; if not, it is ∅. Nothing else is possible.

questions.q: A DFA accepts the empty string λ if and only if:
questions.explain: On λ the machine reads nothing and stays in q0, so the answer depends only on whether q0 is final.

questions.q: In any DFA for the language a⁺b⁺ (one or more a's followed by one or more b's), the initial state must not be final.
questions.explain: λ is not in a⁺b⁺, and a DFA accepts λ exactly when q0 is final, so q0 must not be final.

questions.q: If every state of a DFA is final, the DFA accepts every string over its alphabet.
questions.explain: δ is defined everywhere, so every string ends in some state, and every state is final. Such a DFA could be minimized to one final state that loops on every symbol.

questions.q: Which regular expression describes the strings over {a, b} that have an odd number of a's?
choices: b* a b* (a b* a b*)*
questions.explain: b* a b* gives exactly one a. Each (a b* a b*) block adds two more, so the total is 1 + 2k, which is always odd. The other choices allow any positive number of a's, only even numbers of a's, or force the string to start and end with a.

questions.q: Which string does NOT match the regular expression b* a b* (a b* a b*)*?
questions.explain: The expression matches exactly the strings with an odd number of a's. aab has two a's. ab and bab have one, and aaa has three (one a, then one block aa).

questions.q: Which regular expression describes the strings over {a, b} that begin with aa?
questions.explain: aa(a ∪ b)* forces aa at the start and allows anything after. (a ∪ b)*aa(a ∪ b)* is the language of strings that contain aa anywhere.

questions.q: Over Σ = {a, b}, what language does the regular expression a* b* (a ∪ b)* describe?
choices: Strings with all a's before b's
Strings that end in a or b
Strings with at least one symbol
questions.explain: (a ∪ b)* by itself already gives every string, including λ, so the prefix a* b* adds nothing. The language is Σ*.

questions.q: Languages described by regular expressions and languages accepted by DFAs are both regular languages.
questions.explain: Both describe the regular languages, so for such a language you can either design a DFA or write a regular expression.

questions.q: A DFA for strings over {a, b} that begin with aa has q0 (read nothing), q1 (read a), q2 (read aa, final), and a trap state. Why can't q1 also be final?
choices: Then δ would not be a function
questions.explain: Reading a moves the machine from q0 to q1. If q1 were final, the string a would be accepted, but a does not begin with aa.

questions.q: In a DFA for strings over {a, b} that contain aa as a substring, q0 -a→ q1 -a→ q2 spells out aa, and q2 is final. Where should the b arrow from q1 go?
choices: Back to q0, since the pattern is broken
To a trap state, since acceptance is impossible
Stay in q1, waiting for another a
questions.explain: An a followed by b breaks the aa pattern, so the search starts over in q0. A trap would wrongly reject abaa, staying in q1 would wrongly accept aba, and going to q2 would wrongly accept ab.

questions.q: A DFA for strings over {a, b} that contain aa as a substring needs a trap state.
questions.explain: No prefix makes acceptance impossible: any string can still have aa appended. So there is no state from which the string must be rejected.

questions.q: Which statements about a trap (dead) state are true?
choices: It loops to itself on every symbol
Once the machine enters it, it never leaves
It must be the initial state
questions.explain: A trap state is non-final and loops on every symbol, so any string that reaches it is rejected. It is only needed when some prefix makes acceptance impossible.

questions.q: A DFA for a* ∪ b* (strings that never mix a's and b's) has δ(q0, a) = q1, δ(q0, b) = q2, δ(q1, a) = q1, δ(q1, b) = q3, δ(q2, a) = q3, δ(q2, b) = q2, and q3 loops on both symbols. Which states must be final?
questions.explain: q0 must be final because λ is in the language. q1 (only a's so far) and q2 (only b's so far) are final. q3 is the trap for mixed strings.

questions.q: A DFA for strings over {a, b} that begin with ab has δ(q0, a) = q1 and δ(q0, b) = trap. Where should the a arrow from q1 go?
questions.explain: A string starting with aa can never begin with ab, so it must be rejected for good. Back to q0 would wrongly accept aaab, staying in q1 would wrongly accept aab, and going to q2 would wrongly accept aa.

questions.q: For a given regular language, there is exactly one correct DFA.
questions.explain: Designs are not unique. A DFA may have extra, redundant states, much like working code that is not optimized, and it can be minimized later.

questions.q: Over Σ = {a, b}, any language other than Σ* and ∅ needs a DFA with at least how many states?
questions.explain: A one-state DFA can only accept everything (state final) or nothing (state not final), so any other language needs at least two states.

questions.q: In the DFA for strings that contain aa (q0 -a→ q1 -a→ q2, q1 -b→ q0, q0 loops on b, q2 final and loops on both), what does being in q1 tell you?
choices: It just read an a and has not yet seen aa
It has already seen aa somewhere in the input
It has read only b's so far
It has read an odd number of a's so far
questions.explain: The only way into q1 is reading an a from q0, and q0 means aa has not appeared yet. Once aa is seen the machine is in q2 for good.

questions.q: A DFA's only memory of the input it has read so far is the state it is currently in.
questions.explain: The current state is the machine's only memory. Since a DFA has finitely many states, its memory is finite and very limited.

questions.q: How does a Turing machine's memory differ from a DFA's?
choices: Its tape is unbounded in both directions
It has a fixed number of tape cells
It can only remember the last symbol
It stores the input in its states
questions.explain: A Turing machine's tape is unrestricted in both directions, so its memory is unlimited. A real computer is treated as a Turing machine by assuming unlimited memory, since more disk space can always be added.

questions.q: A Turing machine can do more than accept or reject: it can solve a problem and leave the solution on its tape.
questions.explain: A DFA used as a language acceptor only says accept or reject. A Turing machine can also compute a result and write it on its tape.
